title: Tabbouleh
subtitle: bulgur wheat salad with parsley and tomato
excerpt: A fresh, herb-forward salad with soaked bulgur wheat, masses of flat-leaf parsley, mint, tomato, and a sharp lemon dressing. The parsley is the main ingredient, not the grain. Very simple, very good.
sourceNotes: Tabbouleh is a Lebanese salad eaten across the Levant. In its homeland, the parsley-to-grain ratio is heavily weighted toward parsley. Western versions often invert this and use more grain.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 2 hours ahead. The bulgur soaks up the dressing and the flavour improves.

content.text: Use very fine bulgur wheat and soak it in the lemon juice rather than water. This seasons it from the start. Chop the parsley by hand -- a processor turns it to mush.

items.prepNote: use a large handful of fresh mint leaves, finely chopped

content.text: Put the bulgur wheat in a bowl. Pour over enough boiling water to cover by 2cm. Cover and leave for 20 minutes until absorbed and tender.
Fluff with a fork. Squeeze out any excess water and spread on a clean cloth to dry slightly.
Mix the tomatoes, parsley, mint, and spring onion in a large bowl.
Add the bulgur wheat. Pour over the lemon juice and olive oil.
Toss well and season with salt. Taste and add more lemon or salt as needed.
Rest for 20 minutes before serving for the flavours to develop.

items.symptom: Tabbouleh is too wet and mushy
items.cause: Tomatoes not deseeded or bulgur too wet
items.fix: Deseed the tomatoes and squeeze out their juice. Dry the soaked bulgur well before mixing.

items.symptom: Bulgur is still hard after soaking
items.cause: Not enough boiling water or too short a soak
items.fix: Pour over more boiling water and cover for another 10 minutes. Fine bulgur should soften in 20 minutes.
Add more lemon juice and taste again. Tabbouleh should be bright and sharp.

content.text: Tabbouleh is a defining dish of Lebanese cooking. It is eaten across the Levant -- in Syria, Palestine, Jordan, and beyond. In Lebanon, the dish is very parsley-heavy. The grain is present but secondary. Outside the region, this ratio is often reversed. Traditional versions are eaten on a leaf of romaine lettuce and picked up by hand.
